lessons.title: Huge pages and transparent huge pages
lessons.goal:
Learn why the kernel has 2 MB pages next to 4 KB pages, the two ways to use them (explicit and transparent), and how to see which one a process got.

Why it matters: huge pages speed up large-memory programs (databases, JVMs), but transparent huge pages can cause latency spikes and memory bloat. Many database vendors tell you to turn them off.

setup.note: Programs are small C files. Steps with sudo read kernel data or reserve a few huge pages and release them again.

steps.title: Why bigger pages
steps.text: Every memory access needs a translation from virtual to physical address. The CPU caches recent translations in the **TLB**, which has few entries. With 4 KB pages a 64 GB database needs 16 million translations; with 2 MB pages only 32 000. Fewer TLB misses means less time spent walking page tables.

run.output:
AnonHugePages:   1159168 kB
HugePages_Total:       0
HugePages_Free:        0
Hugepagesize:       2048 kB

steps.title: Explicit huge pages (hugetlbfs)
steps.text: You can **reserve** huge pages in advance with `vm.nr_hugepages`. They are taken from RAM at once, cannot be swapped, and programs must ask for them on purpose (`MAP_HUGETLB` or a hugetlbfs mount). We reserve 4 and release them again.

steps.title: Transparent huge pages (THP)
steps.text: With THP the kernel **automatically** backs aligned 2 MB regions with a huge page when a program touches them, and `khugepaged` merges small pages later. The mode is in `/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled`: `always`, `madvise` (only regions the program asks for) or `never`.

steps.title: See it in a process
steps.text: This program maps 64 MB aligned to 2 MB twice: once telling the kernel `MADV_NOHUGEPAGE`, once `MADV_HUGEPAGE`. After touching the memory it reads `AnonHugePages` from the process's `smaps_rollup`.
steps.under: A fault in a THP-eligible region allocates a whole 2 MB page and zeroes all of it. That can take milliseconds if memory is fragmented and the kernel must **compact** memory first (`defrag`). It also means a program that touches one byte can consume 2 MB. These costs are the source of the "disable THP" advice for latency-sensitive databases.

steps.title: Disabling THP
steps.text: To change it at run time, write to the sysfs file. To make it permanent use the kernel parameter `transparent_hugepage=madvise` (or `never`) or a tuned profile. The setting is lost at reboot otherwise.

run.reason: changes a system-wide setting of this machine; shown as the command you would run

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of huge pages?
options: Fewer TLB misses and smaller page tables

quiz.q: How do explicit huge pages differ from THP?
options: Explicit ones are reserved in advance; THP is automatic
quiz.explain: Reserved with nr_hugepages vs. created on demand.

quiz.q: Which `enabled` mode gives huge pages only where a program asks?
Why do some databases recommend disabling THP?
options: Allocation and compaction stalls cause latency spikes
quiz.explain: Page faults can stall while the kernel compacts memory.

check.scenario: After a kernel update a latency-sensitive Redis shows 200 ms spikes. `AnonHugePages` is large. What do you try?
check.answer: Set THP to `madvise` or `never` (`echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled`, persistently via the boot parameter or tuned), restart Redis and compare latency. Redis itself warns about THP at startup for this reason.

lessons.title: /proc/PID/smaps, finding leaks, and NUMA
lessons.goal:
Learn to read a process's memory map in detail, to find a leak by watching resident size over time, and to see what NUMA means on a machine.

Why it matters: `ps` gives one number. `smaps` tells you whether memory is heap, shared libraries or mapped files, private or shared. This is how you separate a real leak from normal behaviour.

setup.note: Programs are small C files. Steps with sudo read kernel data or reserve a few huge pages and release them again.

steps.title: The memory map
steps.text: `pmap` (or `/proc/PID/maps`) lists each mapped region: address, size, permissions and what backs it (a file, `[heap]`, `[stack]` or nothing for anonymous memory).

run.output:
3464477:   bash --noprofile --norc --noediting -i
Address           Kbytes     RSS   Dirty Mode  Mapping
0000aaaad9040000    1260    1084       0 r-x-- bash
0000aaaad918c000      16      16      16 r---- bash
0000aaaad9190000      36      36      36 rw--- bash
0000aaaad9199000      44      20      20 rw---   [ anon ]

steps.title: smaps: details per region
steps.text: `/proc/PID/smaps` repeats every region with counters: `Rss`, `Pss`, `Shared_Clean`, `Private_Dirty`, `Anonymous` and more. `smaps_rollup` sums them for the whole process. The key split: **private dirty / anonymous** memory is what the process really owns.

run.output:
Rss:                7096 kB
Pss:                1471 kB
Shared_Clean:       6720 kB
Private_Clean:        64 kB
Private_Dirty:       312 kB
Anonymous:           312 kB

steps.title: A leaking program
steps.text: `leak.c` allocates 1 MB every 100 ms and never frees. After three seconds it stops allocating and sleeps.

steps.title: Watch RSS grow
steps.text: A leak is **steady growth of RSS (or anonymous memory) over time** with no matching workload growth. Sample it a few times.

run.cmd: ./leak & p=$!; for i in 1 2 3 4; do sleep 1; echo "t=${i}s RSS: $(ps -o rss= -p $p) kB"; done; kill $p 2>/dev/null
run.output:
[1] 3464529
t=1s RSS: 12360 kB
t=2s RSS: 22640 kB
t=3s RSS: 31892 kB
t=4s RSS: 31892 kB

steps.under: A leak in a C program is memory that is allocated and no longer reachable. Tools: `valgrind --leak-check=full`, `ltrace -e malloc+free`, address sanitizer, or eBPF `memleak-bpfcc`. In garbage-collected languages growth with a stable live set is usually a retention bug (a cache or list that is never trimmed).

steps.title: NUMA
steps.text: On multi-socket servers each CPU has memory attached close to it (**NUMA node**). Access to another node's memory is slower. This VM has one node, but the commands are the same everywhere.

run.output:
available: 1 nodes (0)
node 0 cpus: 0
node 0 size: 5642 MB

has_cpu
has_generic_initiator
has_memory
has_normal_memory
node0
online
possible
power
uevent

quiz.q: Which counter tells you how much memory a process owns privately and has modified?
quiz.explain: These pages belong to the process alone.

quiz.q: What is the typical sign of a leak?
options: RSS grows steadily over time without workload growth

quiz.q: What does NUMA mean for performance?
options: All memory has the same speed
Memory attached to another CPU node is slower to access

quiz.q: Which file sums the smaps counters for a whole process?

check.scenario: A Java service's RSS grows by 50 MB per hour but the heap graph is flat. Where do you look?
check.answer: At memory outside the Java heap: native allocations (direct buffers, JNI, thread stacks), glibc malloc arenas fragmentation (try `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`), and mapped files. Use `pmap -x`/`smaps` to see which regions grow, and JVM Native Memory Tracking (`-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`).

lessons.title: The slab allocator: kernel memory and slabtop
lessons.goal:
Learn how the kernel allocates its own small objects (inodes, dentries, network buffers) and how to see which kind of object uses memory.

Why it matters: when `free` shows memory used but no process owns it, the answer is often the kernel's slab caches (for example millions of cached directory entries).

setup.note: Programs are small C files. Steps with sudo read kernel data or reserve a few huge pages and release them again.

steps.title: Slab in meminfo
steps.text: The kernel allocates many small, fixed-size objects. A **slab cache** keeps pages of these objects ready so allocation is fast and memory does not fragment. `Slab` is the total, `SReclaimable` can be freed under pressure, `SUnreclaim` cannot.

run.output:
Slab: 251 MB
SReclaimable: 109 MB
SUnreclaim: 142 MB

steps.title: slabtop
steps.text: `slabtop` lists the caches sorted by size. It needs root. Names tell the object: `dentry` (directory entries), `inode_cache`, `kmalloc-64` (general 64-byte allocations), `vm_area_struct` (memory mappings).
steps.after: Columns: OBJS (objects), ACTIVE, USE (percent in use), CACHE SIZE, NAME. The top entries differ from machine to machine.

steps.title: Make a cache grow
steps.text: Every file or directory entry we touch creates a **dentry** (cached name) and often an inode object. We create 20 000 empty files in `/dev/shm` (a RAM file system) and compare the object count of the `dentry` cache before and after.

run.cmd: mkdir -p /dev/shm/lab && cd /dev/shm/lab && seq 1 20000 | xargs touch && cd /tmp/lab

steps.under: The slab allocator (SLUB in current kernels) keeps one cache per object type and size. Each cache holds slabs: contiguous pages cut into equal slots. Freed objects go back to the slab for quick reuse. Under memory pressure the kernel's shrinkers ask caches such as dentry and inode to release unused entries (`SReclaimable`).

steps.title: Dropping the reclaimable caches
steps.text: Writing to `drop_caches` asks the kernel to free reclaimable slab objects and page cache. This is a diagnostic tool, not a tuning knob: it throws away useful cache and slows the next reads.

run.cmd: echo 2 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches > /dev/null; sudo grep -E '^dentry ' /proc/slabinfo | awk '{print "after: ", $2}'

options: A pool of equal-sized kernel objects
quiz.explain: It makes small kernel allocations fast.

quiz.q: Which `meminfo` field cannot be freed under memory pressure?
Which tool lists slab caches by size?

options: A directory entry cache object (name to inode)
quiz.explain: The VFS caches path components as dentries.

check.scenario: `free` says 20 GB used, but `ps` shows processes using only 6 GB. How do you find the rest?
check.answer: Look at the kernel: `grep -E 'Slab|SUnreclaim|PageTables|KernelStack' /proc/meminfo` and `sudo slabtop -o -s c`. A huge `dentry`/`inode_cache` or network object count (for example from millions of small files or sockets) explains it. Also check shared memory (`Shmem`, tmpfs), and page cache.

interview.q: What are huge pages and why use them?
interview.a: 2 MB (or 1 GB) pages instead of 4 KB. They reduce TLB misses and page-table size, which speeds up programs with large memory. See [the lesson](#/lesson/16/hugepages-thp).

interview.q: Why is THP sometimes disabled for databases?
interview.a: Allocation and compaction of 2 MB pages can stall the process and cause latency spikes; memory use can also bloat. Many databases recommend `madvise` or `never`.

interview.q: How do you tell a leak from a large but stable footprint?
interview.a: Watch RSS or private/anonymous memory over time: steady growth without workload growth is a leak. VSZ alone is not evidence. See [the lesson](#/lesson/16/smaps-leaks-numa).
Non-uniform memory access: each CPU socket has local memory; remote memory is slower. Use `numactl`, `numastat` and memory policy to keep processes close to their memory.

interview.q: Where does memory go that no process owns?
interview.a: Kernel memory: slab caches (dentries, inodes, network buffers), page tables, kernel stacks, tmpfs/shmem, and the page cache. See [the slab lesson](#/lesson/16/slab-allocator).
Slab memory the kernel can free under pressure, mostly dentry and inode caches.

glossary.def: Translation Lookaside Buffer: the CPU cache of virtual-to-physical page translations.
A 2 MB (or 1 GB) memory page used instead of many 4 KB pages.
Transparent Huge Pages: automatic use of huge pages by the kernel.
Proportional set size: a process's memory with shared pages divided by the number of sharers.
Non-uniform memory access: memory speed depends on which CPU accesses it.
Kernel allocator that keeps pools of equal-sized objects.
A cached directory entry that maps a name to an inode.
